title: San Juan County CO well depth and cost
meta_description: San Juan County wells have a 100 ft median depth and 11 gpm median yield. See drilling costs, water levels, and risks for mountain properties.
h1: Water wells in San Juan County, Colorado
intro_html:
San Juan County is classic high-country drilling: fractured bedrock, short building seasons, and a wide spread in well depths from one parcel to the next. State records show 243 permitted wells here, with enough data to get a reasonable feel for how deep you’re likely to drill and how much water you can expect.

If you’re looking at land near Silverton or out in the backcountry, it pays to look closely at neighboring well logs and plan for mountain drilling costs. Here’s what the state data actually shows for this county.

sections.heading: How deep are wells in San Juan County
sections.html:
Based on reported completions, the median well depth in San Juan County is about 100 feet. The middle half of wells fall between 58 and 200 feet, so most drillers will bid with a wide allowance to cover that full range in fractured bedrock.

There are wells as deep as 319 feet in the 90th percentile, and the deepest on record reaches 480 feet. About 47% of wells stop under 100 feet, 39% land between 100 and 300 feet, and 14% run 300–600 feet. In this kind of granite and gneiss, the driller is chasing water-bearing fractures, so depth can change quickly from one ridge or valley to the next.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you can expect
sections.html:
On the production side, San Juan County actually looks pretty solid for mountain bedrock. The median reported yield is 11.0 gpm, with the middle half between 7.4 and 15.0 gpm. That’s more than enough for a typical exempt household well, which is limited to 35 gpm pumping anyway.

None of the reported wells came in under 1 gpm, 12% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, 46% fall between 5 and 15 gpm, and 42% exceed 15 gpm. That’s a strong distribution, but remember only 24 wells report yield, so you should still treat each new hole as a fresh gamble in fractured rock.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they suggest
sections.html:
Only 16 wells report a static water level, so the picture is limited, but the numbers are encouraging. The median depth to water is about 40 feet, and the middle half of readings sit between 7 and 52 feet below ground. That means many wells have water standing relatively high in the casing.

With so few measurements, and likely taken at different times and seasons, you can’t read any clear long-term trend up or down. Think of this as a snapshot: expect water to be encountered fairly shallow in many spots, but drilled depth still needs to reach and secure a decent fracture zone for year-round supply.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and when
sections.html:
Drilling in San Juan County has come in waves. Records show 7 permits in the 1970s, then a jump to 51 in the 1980s. Activity tapered to 29 in the 1990s, ticked up to 33 in the 2000s, then rose again with 49 permits in the 2010s and 47 already in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025.

Most wells are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with a handful in alluvial deposits and one in the Hermosa formation. Authorized (Pe, Pg) shows up on 35 wells, with Dak Drilling LLC and McCracken Well Drilling Inc each on 10 wells. That history tells you local drillers know they’re working complex hard rock, not the Denver Basin.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
In San Juan County’s fractured mountain bedrock, typical drilling rates run around $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, that puts the bare hole itself in the ballpark of $6,500–$10,000.

By the time you add steel or PVC casing, grout, pitless adapter, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished residential well usually lands around $12,500–$22,000 at that same median depth. If your site ends up closer to the 200–300 foot range that many wells reach, you should budget proportionally higher and confirm with a local driller who’s worked nearby properties.

sections.heading: Environmental and water-supply risks to check
sections.html:
San Juan County’s mining history shows up in the data: within about 10 miles there are 9,581 historic mine features, 33 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 14 PFAS sampling or contamination locations. That doesn’t mean your well is unsafe, but it does mean water-quality testing is not optional.

Most wells tap fractured bedrock, which can transmit contaminants along cracks. Before you buy, pull the well permit and any test results, and plan on a full lab panel for metals and other pollutants. Also, with only 92 wells reporting depth and 24 reporting yield, there’s still real risk of a low producer or a dry hole on marginal sites. Layout your septic and building envelope to keep good separation from the well.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a San Juan County well
sections.html:
When you’re evaluating a parcel in San Juan County or around Silverton, start by pulling nearby well logs and looking at the depth spread: the middle half from 58 to 200 feet, with some much deeper, is what should drive your budget. Assume fractured bedrock, not a uniform aquifer.

Most existing permits are for domestic/household use, with stock, irrigation, and a large block of monitoring wells also in the records. For a new home, plan on an exempt household well unless you’re in an area needing augmentation. Make your offer on land contingent on a successful well and acceptable water quality, and line up a driller early so you’re not trying to punch a hole at the wrong time of year.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in San Juan County, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported wells in San Juan County have a median depth of about 100 feet, with the middle half between 58 and 200 feet. The 90th percentile sits at 319 feet, and the deepest well on record is 480 feet. About 47% of wells are under 100 feet, 39% run 100–300 feet, and 14% fall between 300 and 600 feet.

faq.q: How much water do San Juan County wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 24 wells that report pump tests, the median yield is 11.0 gpm, with the middle half between 7.4 and 15.0 gpm. None of the reported wells are under 1 gpm. About 12% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, 46% in the 5–15 gpm range, and 42% produce more than 15 gpm, which is strong for mountain bedrock.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in San Juan County, CO?
faq.a: In San Juan County’s fractured mountain bedrock, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, that means roughly $6,500–$10,000 for the borehole. A complete residential setup with casing, pump, tank, trenching, and electrical commonly totals around $12,500–$22,000 at that depth, with deeper wells costing more.

faq.q: How deep is the water table in San Juan County?
faq.a: Only 16 wells report static water levels, but they suggest fairly shallow standing water in many spots. The median depth to water is around 40 feet, and the middle half of readings run from 7 to 52 feet below ground. Because the dataset is small and readings are from different times, it’s a snapshot rather than a clear long-term trend.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in San Juan County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Records show 9,581 historic mine features, 33 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 14 PFAS sampling or contamination locations within about 10 miles, so testing is important. Many wells are in fractured bedrock, which can carry contaminants along cracks. Always review any past lab results and commission a full water-quality test before relying on a well for drinking water.
